subject: Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA

messages.author: a6af88edba233452
messages.subject: Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA
parts:
Hi, I am working on a model with three regressions (three correlated dependent variables) that are estimated simultaneously and have different independent variables for each regression. They are seemingly unrelated regressions (SUR).
As the estimation through MCMC is taking more time than expected, I would like to know whether I can use INLA as an alternative and if R-INLA allows such kind of estimation.
The examples using R-INLA that I've seen so far usually work only with one regression.

Thanks in advance!

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA
parts:
Hi,

Yes, from what the Wikipedia entry on SURs indicates, one possibility is to model the correlated measurement errors with an "iid3d" latent model. The details of course depend on the details of the model you have, but hopefully this should get you started. As a first step I recommend that you figure out the mathematical definition of your desired model; "shortcut names" like SUR won't tell you directly what a model really looks like.
See the latent models documentation on r-inla.org.

Finn

messages.author: f66907f526d3c7bf
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA
parts:
Finn has already pointed out the iid3d latent model for the error
structure. For the rest, the simplest (but not very elegant) approach
might be to set covariates to the intercept value if they are not
needed, e.g. if you mean-centre everything then set unneeded
continuous covariates to 0, and factors to the first level. You might
want to be careful with the priors: I don't know how sensitive INLA
will be to integrating over vague priors.

An alternative would be to set out the model with a bit more care,
using some of the ideas here: <http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools>.
But unless you're going to be doing more complex stuff in the future,
this might be more hassle than its worth.

Bob
